questions.q: A porter lifts a heavy suitcase of mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>80</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> and at the destination lowers it down by a distance of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>80</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi></math> with a constant velocity. Calculate the work done by the porter in lowering the suitcase. (take <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>8</mn><msup><mrow><mo> </mo><mi>ms</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math> )
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
WPorter +Wmg=ΔK.E.=0
 WPorter =-Wmg=-mgh
=-80×9.8×.8=-627.2 J

questions.q: Which one of the following forces cannot be expressed in terms of potential energy?
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution: Potential energy is defined for conservative force only. It is not defined for non-conservative force i.e. frictional force.

questions.q: A particle moves in $x-y$ plane under the influence of a force $\vec{F}$ such that its linear momentum is $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}(\mathrm{t})=\hat{i} \cos (\mathrm{kt})-\hat{j} \sin (\mathrm{kt})$. If $\mathrm{k}$ is constant, the angle between $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}$ will be :
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}=\cos (\mathrm{kt}) \hat{\mathrm{i}}-\sin (\mathrm{kt}) \hat{\mathrm{j}} ;|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}|=1 \\ & \because \overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}=\mathrm{m} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \\ & \therefore \hat{\mathrm{P}}=\hat{\mathrm{v}} \\ & \Rightarrow \hat{\mathrm{v}}=\cos (\mathrm{kt}) \hat{\mathrm{i}}-\sin (\mathrm{kt}) \hat{\mathrm{j}} \\ & \hat{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{-\mathrm{k} \sin (\mathrm{kt}) \hat{\mathrm{i}}-\mathrm{k} \cos (\mathrm{kt}) \hat{\mathrm{j}}}{\mathrm{k}} \\ & \Rightarrow \hat{\mathrm{a}}=-\sin k t \hat{\mathrm{i}}-\cos \mathrm{kt} \hat{\mathrm{j}} \\ & \because \hat{\mathrm{F}}=\hat{\mathrm{a}}=-\sin \mathrm{kt} \hat{\mathrm{i}}-\cos \mathrm{kt} \hat{\mathrm{j}} \\ & \cos \theta=\frac{\hat{\mathrm{F}} \cdot \hat{\mathrm{P}}}{|\hat{\mathrm{F}}||\hat{\mathrm{P}}|}=-\frac{\sin \mathrm{kt} \cos \mathrm{t}+\sin \mathrm{kt} \cos \mathrm{t}}{1 \times 1}=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A stone tide to a string of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi></math> is whirled in a vertical circle with the other end of the string at the centre. At a certain instant of time, the stone is at its lowest position and has a speed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>u</mi></math>. The magnitude of change in its velocity, as it reaches a position where the string is horizontal, is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msqrt><mi>x</mi><mfenced><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mi>g</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></mfenced></msqrt></math>. The value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi></math> is
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Applying conservation of mechanical energy at the point A and B, we get12mu2+0=12mv2+mgL

⇒v=u2-2gL

Now in vector form. v→i=u i^ and v→f=v j^

Therefore, change in velocity will be,∆V→=vj^-ui^ and ΔV→=u2+v2

⇒ΔV=u2+u2-2gL

=2u2-gL

Hence, x=2

questions.q: Consider a force F→=-xi^+yj^ . The work done by this force in moving a particle from point A1,0 to B0,1 along the line segment is : (all quantities are in SI units)
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
It is given that a force F→=-xi^+yj^ acts on a particle. The particle is moved from point A1,0 to B0,1 along the line segment.

Work done by a variable force on the particle,
W=∫F→·dr→=∫F→·dxi^+dyj^
(In two dimension, dr→=dxi^+dyj^
and it is given F→=-xi^+yj^)

W=∫-xi^+yj^·dxi^+dyj^

=∫-xdx+ydy=∫-xdx+∫ydy.
As the particle is displaced from A1,0 to B0,1, x varies from 1 to 0 and y varies from 0 to 1.
So, work will be,

W=-∫10xdx+∫01ydy=-x2210+y2201

=120+12+12-0=1 J.

questions.q: A small particle of mass m moves in such a way that its potential energy U=12mω2r2 where ω is constant and r is the distance of the particle from origin. Assuming Bohr’s quantization of momentum and circular orbit, the radius of nth orbit will be proportional to
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
The data given is

U=12mω2r2

From Bohr's quantization, 

mvr=nh2π⇒v2=nh2πrm2   ...(i)

In an orbit the value of the kinetic energy is half of the potential energy,

K=mω2r24

Substituting the value of equation (i) in the kinetic energy,

K=12mn2h24π2m2r2=mω2r24⇒n2h22π2m2ω2=r4⇒r∝n

questions.q: A constant power delivering machine has towed a box, which was initially at rest, along a horizontal straight line. The distance moved by the box in time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>t</mi></math> is proportional to :-
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
P=C⇒FV=C⇒MdVdtV=C
⇒V22∝t
⇒V∝t1/2
⇒dxdt∝t1/2
⇒x∝t3/2

questions.q: A body of mass ' \(m\) ' connected to a massless and unstretchable string goes in verticle circle of radius ' \(R\) 'under gravity \(g\). The other end of the string is fixed at the center of circle. If velocity at top of circular path is \(n \sqrt{g R}\), where, \(n \geqslant 1\), then ratio of kinetic energy of the body at bottom to that at top of the circle is
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & v_0=\sqrt{v^2+2 g(2 R)} \\ & v_0=\sqrt{n^2 g R+4 g R} \\ & \therefore \quad \frac{k_{\text {bottom }}}{k_{\text {top }}}=\frac{v_0^2}{v^2}=\frac{n^2+4}{n^2}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A uniform cable of mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>M</mi></math> and length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi></math> is placed on a horizontal surface such that its <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mfenced separators="|"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mfenced><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi></mrow></msup></math> part is hanging below the edge of the surface. To lift the hanging part of the cable upto the surface, the work done should be:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Mass of the part hanging is Mn. Centre of mass of this part lies L2n distance from the surface.

∴ Work done in lifting the hanging part to surface is
W=Mn·gL2n
=MgL2n2

questions.q: A body is released from a height equal to the radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfenced><mi>R</mi></mfenced></math> of the earth. The velocity of the body when it strikes the surface of the earth will be: (Given <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo></math> acceleration due to gravity on the earth.)
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Using conservation of mechanical energy,

Ui+Ki=Uf+Kf

⇒-GMm2R+0=-GMmR+12mv2

⇒12mv2=GMm2R

⇒v=GMR=gR

questions.q: Sand is being dropped from a stationary dropper at a rate of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>5</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> on a conveyor belt moving with a velocity of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>. The power needed to keep belt moving with the same velocity will be
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
When the sand is dropped on the conveyor belt its velocity will become equal to that of the conveyor. Therefore, v=5 m s-1.

The force required to keep the conveyor belt moving will be equal to the gain in the momentum by the sand per second.

⇒F=dmdtv⇒F=0.5×5=2.5 N

Now the power required to keep the conveyor belt moving will be,

P=Fv⇒P=2.5×5=12.5 W.

questions.q: A ball suspended by a thread swings in a vertical plane so that its magnitude of acceleration in the extreme position and lowest position are equal. The angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mi><mo>)</mo></math> of thread deflection in the extreme position will be :
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
At the lowermost point, there is no tangential force on the ball. Thus, there exists no tangential acceleration at the bottommost point, only the centripetal acceleration survives.

On the other hand, in the extreme position of the ball, there is no centripetal acceleration as the ball becomes momentarily at rest at that position. Here, only tangential acceleration survives.

Thus, with respect to the figure above, equating the kinetic energy at the bottommost point to the potential energy at the extreme point, we have
12mv2=mgl(1-cosθ)⇒v2l=2g(1-cosθ)   ...1

Now, the net acceleration at at the extreme point can be written as

at=gsinθ   ...2

According to the given problem, it follows that for the two positions of the ball,

at=v2l   ...3

Equations (1), (2) and (3) imply that

gsinθ=2g(1-cosθ)⇒2sinθ2cosθ2=4sin2θ2⇒tanθ2=12⇒θ=2tan-112

questions.q: A person pushes a box on a rough horizontal plateform surface. He applies a force of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>200</mn><mo> </mo><mi>N</mi></math> over a distance of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>15</mn><mo> </mo><mi>m</mi></math>. Thereafter, he gets progressively tired and his applied force reduces linearly with distance to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>100</mn><mo> </mo><mi>N</mi></math>. The total distance through which the box has been moved is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>30</mn><mo> </mo><mi>m</mi></math>. What is the work done by the person during the total movement of the box?
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
W=area=(200×15)+12(100+200)×15

=3000+2250

W=5250 J

questions.q: A particle moves in one dimension from rest under the influence of a force that varies with the distance traveled by the particle as shown in the figure. The kinetic energy of the particle after it has traveled 3 m is:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Change in K.E.=Work done=Area
Area=(3×2)+(12×1×1)=6.5
∴ Change in kinetic energy=6.5 J

questions.q: A sand dropper drops sand of mass $m(t)$ on a conveyer belt at a rate proportional to the square root of speed $(v)$ of the belt, i.e. $\frac{\mathrm{dm}}{\mathrm{dt}} \propto \sqrt{v}$. If P is the power delivered to run the belt at constant speed then which of the following relationship is true?
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Power $=\vec{F} \cdot \vec{V}$
and $F=\frac{d p}{d t}=$ Rate of change of linear momentum
$F=V \cdot \frac{d m}{d t}=K_1 V^{\frac{3}{2}}, K$ is constant
Power $(P)=\left(K V^{\frac{3}{2}}\right) \cdot(V)=K V^{\frac{5}{2}}$

So, $P^2 \propto V^5$

questions.q: For a particle in uniform circular motion, the acceleration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math> at any point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>P</mi><mfenced><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> on the circular path of radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> is (when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>θ</mi></math> is measured from the positive <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi></math>-axis and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>v</mi></math> is uniform speed):
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Acceleration of a particle in uniform circular motion is directed towards the centre of the circle and its magnitude is v2R. The radius vector isr→=Rcosθi^+Rsinθj^

Therefore, a→=-v2Rr^=v2R−cosθi^−sinθj^

questions.q: Given below is the plot of a potential energy function U(x) for a system, in which a particle is in one dimensional motion, while a conservative force F(x) acts on it. Suppose that Emech =8 J, the incorrect statement for this system is :
options: at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>></mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mo>.</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi></math>. is constant throughout the region.

at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo><</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mo>.</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi></math>. is smallest and the particle is moving at the slowest speed.

at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mo>.</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi></math>. is greatest and the particle is moving at the fastest speed.
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
(A) at x>x4,  U= constant =6 J

K=Emech. -U=2 J= constant

(B) at x<x1,  U= constant =8 J

K=Emech. -U=8-8=0 J

Particle is at rest.

(C) At x=x2,U=0⇒Emech. =K=8 J
KE is greatest, and particle is moving at fastest speed.

(D) At x=x3,  U=4 J

U+K=8 J

K=4 J

questions.q: A block of mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>100</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> slides over a distance of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>10</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> on a horizontal surface. If the co-efficient of friction between the surfaces is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>4</mn></math> , then the work done against friction (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></math>) is:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Given m=100 kg

s=10 m

μ=0.4

The frictional force is given by

 f=μmg=0.4×100×10=400 N

So, the work done by the force can be calculated as follows:

W=f×s=400×10=4000 J

questions.q: In a reactor, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mmultiscripts><mi mathvariant="normal">U</mi><none></none><mn>235</mn><mprescripts></mprescripts><mn>92</mn><none></none></mmultiscripts></math> fuel is fully used up in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>30</mn></math> days. The energy released fission is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>200</mn><mo> </mo><mi>MeV</mi></math>. Given that the Avogadro number, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>023</mn><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>26</mn></msup></math> per kilo mole and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo> </mo><mi>eV</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>19</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></math>. The power output of the reactor is close to:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
P=Et

=2235×6.023×1026×200×1.6×10-1930×24×60×60=60 MW

questions.q:
A body of mass 100 g is moving in circular path of radius 2 m on vertical plane as shown in figure. The velocity of the body at point $A$ is $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The ratio of its kinetic energies at point $B$ and $C$ is :
(Take acceleration due to gravity as $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \times 100+0=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mV}_{\mathrm{B}}^2+\mathrm{mg}\left(\mathrm{R}-\frac{\mathrm{R} \sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ & 100=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{B}}^2+2 \mathrm{gR}\left(1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right] \\ & \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{B}}^2=100-20(2-\sqrt{3}) \\ & \left.\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{B}}^2=60+20 \sqrt{3}\right) \\ & \mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mV}_{\mathrm{B}}^2=\frac{\mathrm{m}}{2}(60+20 \sqrt{3}) \\ & \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}(100)=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mV} \\ & 2 \\ & 100=\mathrm{mg}\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{R}}{2}\right) \\ & 100 \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{C}}^2=60 \\ & \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{C}}^2=40 \\ & \mathrm{~K} . \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mV} \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{C}}^2=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}(40) \\ & \mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{60+20 \sqrt{3}}{40}=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{3+\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A force $\left(3 x^2+2 x-5\right) \mathrm{N}$ displaces a body from $x=2 \mathrm{~m}$ to $x=4 \mathrm{~m}$. Work done by this force is ________ $J$.
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & W=\int_{x_1}^{x_2} F d x \\ & W=\int_2^4\left(3 x^2+2 x-5\right) d x \\ & W=\left[x^3+x^2-5 x\right]_2^4 \\ & W=[60-2] J=58 J\end{aligned}$

questions.q: An object of mass m initially at rest on a smooth horizontal plane starts moving under the action of force F=2 N. In the process of its linear motion, the angle θ (as shown in figure) between the direction of force and horizontal varies as θ=kx, where k is a constant and x is the distance covered by the object from its initial position. The expression of kinetic energy of the object will be E=nksin θ. The value of n is ______.
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
As seen in the free body diagram of the object, normal force N, weight mg and force in parallel and perpendicular directions are acting.

Using Newton's law of motion

Along horizontal direction, Fcosθ=ma

⇒2cos(kx)=mvdvdx

Integrating the above relation, we have

∫0vvdv=2∫0xcos(kx)dx

⇒mv22=2ksinkx

Thus, kinetic energy of the object will be K.E.=2ksinθ

Thus, the value of n=2.

questions.q: A body of mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> is driven by an engine delivering a constant power of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>. the body starts from rest and moves in a straight line. After <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>9</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></math>, the body has moved a distance (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math>)….
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Given,

Power delivered by the engine P=1 J s-1

Mass of the body is m= 2 kg 

Body starts from the rest, u=0

Using work energy Theorem, 

W=∆K=Pt

Pt=12mv2-0

Substitute the values in the above equation, we get
(1)t=12×2×v2
⇒v=t=dsdt
⇒∫0tds=∫09tdt

⇒s=93232=23×27

⇒s=18 m

questions.q: A small bob tied at one end of a thin string of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> is describing a vertical circle so that the maximum and minimum tension in the string is in the ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn><mo>:</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. The velocity of the bob at the highest position is ______ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>. (Take <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math>)
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Let the speed of bob at lowest position be v1 and at the highest position be v2.

Maximum tension is at lowest position and minimum tension is at the highest position.
Now, using, conservation of mechanical energy,

12mv12=12mv22+mg2l

⇒  v12=v22+4 gl   ....1

Now, Tmax-mg=mv12l

⇒ Tmax=mg+mv12l

&  Tmin+mg=mv22l

⇒ Tmin=mv22l-mg

TmaxTmin=51

⇒  mg+mv12lmv22l-mg=51

⇒ mg+mv12l=mv22l-mg5

⇒ mg+mlv22+4 gl=5mv22l-5mg

⇒ mg+mv22l+4mg=5mv22l-5mg

⇒ 10 mg=4mv22l

v2=10×10×14

Thus, the velocity of the bob at the highest position is 5 m s-1.

questions.q: A force $\mathrm{f}=\mathrm{x}^2 \mathrm{y} \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\mathrm{y}^2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}$ acts on a particle in a plane $\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y}=10$. The work done by this force during a displacement from $(0,0)$ to $(4 \mathrm{~m}, 2 \mathrm{~m})$ is $\qquad$ Joule (round off to the nearest integer)
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & y=10-x \\ & w=\int_0^4 x^2(10-x) d x+\int_0^2 y^2 d y \\ & =\frac{10 x^3}{3}-\left.\frac{x^4}{4}\right|_0 ^4+\left.\frac{y^3}{3}\right|_0 ^2 \\ & =\frac{640}{3}-\frac{256}{4}+\frac{8}{3} \\ & =216 \times 64 \\ & =152 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$
